rows.note: Named explicitly in published postings across categories: Barclays QA dev ('C++ and scripting languages (Python)'), UBS electronic-trading QA ('proficient in data analysis using... Python or equivalent'), Two Sigma software engineer, and Optiver's official interview guide ('C++, Java, or Python'). Bloomberg publishes Python tooling (memray) but its hiring requirements were not verifiable in this pass.

Barclays requires 'excellent programming skills in C++' (quant dev) and 'C++ and Python for quantitative finance applications' (rates QA); UBS says 'especially C++ or Python'; Citadel Securities' posting names C++ experience. Bloomberg's open-source core (BDE, BlazingMQ) is C++-centric, supporting C++ as the market-data priority.

Optiver's published guide stresses standard data structures, their time/space complexity and implementation-level detail for 'performance-essential applications'. Bank postings describe model/analytics library development on shared codebases; exact bank interview formats are community-reported (unverified).

Jane Street officially publishes a Probability & Markets Guide and says trading interviews test collaborative problem solving, not finance knowledge; UBS rates QA expects stochastic modelling foundations. Probability is the most consistently published quantitative bar for trading-side seats.

Barclays QA accountabilities include 'in-depth research, data analysis, and statistical modelling'; UBS e-trading QA is built around data analysis and TCA; Two Sigma's engineering posting assumes statistics-adjacent quantitative finance concepts. Bloomberg's data-engineering family also leans on it (inferred).

Two Sigma's official posting explicitly requires 'understanding of mathematical concepts in quantitative finance including Linear [algebra]...'; for banks it is implicit in pricing/risk work rather than always named; prop-trading postings emphasise probability over linear algebra.

Barclays rates QA names 'Numerical methods, nonlinear analytics, and production-grade library development' and stochastic-rate model work; UBS rates QA expects calibration experience — both published. Rarely named in prop-trading or market-data postings reviewed.

Banks publish domain bars: UBS wants 'understanding of financial products and markets, especially interest rate derivatives'; Barclays rates QA wants US rates products and the quant-dev posting asks 'willingness to learn financial mathematics'. Jane Street states the opposite policy ('We won't test you on knowledge of finance or economics'), hence desirable for prop trading.

Citadel Securities' posting requires 'experience with distributed systems'; Two Sigma's engineering duties include simulation orchestration frameworks; Barclays values 'distributed systems (Symphony/Kafka/Redis)'; Bloomberg's self-description is large-scale, high-availability computing. Interview formats themselves are not published.

Two Sigma's posting requires SQL and relational-database concepts; UBS e-trading QA requires 'extracting data via e.g. SQL' and tick stores (KDB/OneTick); Bloomberg maintains its own database (Comdb2), indicating data-store depth in market-data engineering (inferred for hiring bars).

Optiver's guide names 'computer architecture, networking, concurrency and memory management' and performance-essential systems; Citadel Securities builds 'one of the world's most powerful trading platforms' with low-latency demands; UBS e-trading QA specifies 'low latency trading strategies' (published); Bloomberg describes itself as 'high-availability, low-latency' — essential only where the seat is latency-critical.

Optiver's published interview guide lists networking fundamentals among topics to revise; Bloomberg's messaging infrastructure (BlazingMQ, amqpprox) implies protocol/transport fluency for infrastructure roles (inferred for hiring bars). Seldom named in asset-manager or bank postings reviewed.

Jane Street runs a dedicated ML discipline with realistic modelling interviews; Two Sigma and BlackRock profiles are ML-heavy. UBS names ML twice in published postings (rates QA: 'machine learning techniques'; e-trading: ML 'in a controlled and practical way'), and UBS declares firmwide AI ambitions — but ML is not universal across bank quant seats.

Two Sigma's posting requires Linux/Unix plus testing frameworks; Barclays names 'cross platform (Linux RHEL/Windows) applications'; Jane Street tells technology candidates to be 'comfortable with your own setup and tools of choice' (published). Bloomberg's stack is Linux-centred (inferred).
